hints: Focus on what the hydroxide ion actually does in nucleophilic substitution, not just on how fast the reaction is.
Notice that $\text{OH}^-$ has lone pairs and forms a new $\text{C-O}$ bond to carbon in both the primary and tertiary case.
Compare this shared nucleophile role with features that are different, like carbocation formation and number of steps, to pick the statement true for both.
walkthrough:
**Recall what SN2 means**

Think of SN2 as one smooth, concerted attack. The nucleophile comes in as the leaving group leaves.

Chemical idea:
$$\text{HO}^- + \text{C-Br} \rightarrow [\text{HO} \cdots \text{C} \cdots \text{Br}]^{\ddagger} \rightarrow \text{C-OH} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Recall what SN1 means**

Think of SN1 as two separate stages. First the $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks to give a carbocation, then the nucleophile attacks.

Chemical idea:
$$\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-Br} \rightarrow \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+ + \text{Br}^- \text{ then } \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-OH}$$

**Spot the common role of hydroxide**

In both mechanisms $\text{OH}^-$ uses a lone pair to donate to an electron-deficient carbon to make the $\text{C-O}$ bond. That is exactly what a nucleophile, an electron pair donor, does.

**Check why the other features are not shared**

Only SN1 makes a full $\text{C}^+$ intermediate, only SN2 is one step, and both use heterolytic (not homolytic) fission to give $\text{Br}^-$. So the only statement true for both is the nucleophile role.

options.A: Incorrect. Both reactions break $\text{C-Br}$ heterolytically, with both bonding electrons going to bromine to form $\text{Br}^-$. Homolytic fission would give radicals, which does not happen here.
options.B: Correct. In both SN1 and SN2, $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a nucleophile. It donates an electron pair to carbon to form the $\text{C-OH}$ bond, either in the single SN2 step or in the second SN1 step after the carbocation forms.
options.C: Incorrect. Only the SN1 reaction of $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$ forms a positively charged intermediate, the tertiary carbocation $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$. The SN2 reaction goes through a single transition state with no carbocation intermediate.
options.D: Incorrect. Only the SN2 reaction of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ occurs in a single concerted step. The SN1 reaction occurs in two steps, slow ionisation followed by fast attack by $\text{OH}^-$.
